title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hookLine: the gods churn the ocean, poison rises first, and Shiva drinks it; why devotees stay up all night
carry: nilakantha: god takes the poison so others live
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
last: HOLI IS KRISHNA'S PLAY, AND EVERYONE'S INVITED.

lines: THE NIGHT HE DRANK THE DANGER.
cards: Look closely at many images of Shiva, and his throat is a darker blue than the rest of him. It isn't a painting mistake; it's a scar, of a kind. One of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated.
And one story people tell about Maha Shivaratri is how his throat got that color: a moment when the whole universe nearly ended, and one god drank the danger so everyone else could live.

teach.b: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. The gods and the demons, usually enemies, agree to work together for once. They want amrita, the nectar of immortality, at the bottom of the ocean of milk.
So they churn the ocean, the samudra manthan, with the mountain Mandara as the churning stick and the great serpent Vasuki as the rope, gods pulling one end, demons the other.
But the first thing that rises isn't nectar. It's poison: Halahala, so strong its fumes spread in every direction and begin to burn the worlds. Gods, demons, every creature, run to Shiva.
The text says Shiva looks on them with compassion, and his wife, the Goddess, agrees. He gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it.
And in the telling many know, he holds it in his throat, not swallowed, not spat out, and his throat turns blue. That's the teaching in the blue throat.
Shiva is Mahadeva, the great god, and here greatness means this: when the poison comes, he's the one who takes it in, so the world can live. Devotees answer him on Shivaratri.
Many fast, stay awake through the night, and pour water and milk over the lingam, chanting Om Namah Shivaya.

teach.h: GOD TAKES THE POISON SO OTHERS LIVE.
teach.b: Some say the vigil echoes the churning, when the gods stayed up singing to Shiva while he held the poison; some say the cool water soothes his burning throat. These are explanations people give, among several.
But the shape is clear: God held the hard thing for us, and for one night, we stay up with him.

how: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus keep vigil at Shiva temples through the night, chanting and offering water, milk and bilva leaves to the lingam; some connect the night with Shiva drinking the poison from the churned ocean.

o: a spring day of throwing colored powder in the streets
the nine nights honoring the Goddess in her nine forms
Shiva's great night, kept awake, for the god who held the poison

p: the mountain used as the churning stick
the serpent used as the rope

s: the first thing to rise from the churned ocean is the nectar
the poison halahala rises first, and begins to burn the worlds.
gods and demons pull together on the serpent rope
for once, they work together, one at each end.
in a well-known telling, Shiva holds the poison in his throat
neither swallowing nor spitting it out, so his throat turns blue.

games.q: a friend asks why anyone stays up all night on Shivaratri. by today's story, what fits?
o: Shiva held the world's poison for everyone; many devotees keep vigil with him in thanks.
staying awake earns extra luck for the year ahead.
it's only a party that happens to have a god's name.
games.why: devotees fast, chant Om Namah Shivaya and pour water on the lingam through the night. one reading: the gods once kept vigil while he held the poison.

practice: If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya slowly, with your breath, the way devotees chant it through the night. If you don't, simply breathe.
Then bring to mind one person you love who's holding something hard right now, something they can't swallow and can't spit out: a worry, a grief. Don't fix it.
Keep them company in it for a few breaths, the way devotees keep Shiva company.

wordCard.voice: Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, the blue-throated one, who held the world's poison so others could live.

orig.note: Sanskrit nīla (blue) + kaṇṭha (throat): Shiva, the blue-throated.
